headline: Felipe deber har face à deep reforms
content: Spain faces another change. While recently bidding farewell to former President Adolfo Suárez, now it says goodbye to King Juan Carlos I. This month reigns again a monarch born in Spain—as opposed to Juan Carlos who was born in Rome—and reigns alongside his consort, Letizia Ortiz—an asturian commoner unlike Queen Sofía—who has royal relatives everywhere. And their daughter, Princess Leonor, becomes heir presumptive provided legal processes accelerate gender equality before she assumes title. Changes also affect Latin America? Probably not significantly. The Prince Philip served as Spain’s representative at presidential inaugurations across Latin America—the last being in El Salvador where might someone else take over after him? Perhaps Colombia or Panama could welcome King Felipe VI first should schedules remain unchanged—even Mexican president Enrique Peña Nieto might greet the new king soon. But grandfather Juan Carlos’ decision affects young Leonor too, still far off representing both country and award ceremonies bearing her name starting late June pending legislative changes favoring women heirs above male counterparts. Meanwhile, Britain’s Queen Elizabeth II remains merely an observer amidst political shifts worldwide despite turning eighty-eight years old herself while marking sixty-one years upon ascending British throne yesterday morning.
